incident.title: [DEMO C043] Slack user actions fail despite configured bot permissions
incident.description: A Slack workflow using a user token fails with a missing_scope error despite the expected permission being configured, while bot posting continues to work.

tasks.question: Scope and coordinate the evidence-led incident investigation.

Using null-filter queries first, what canonical executor records exist for the failed Slack user-token actions between 2026-11-12T09:50:00Z and 2026-11-12T10:15:00Z, including exact error payloads (for example missing_scope), request/connection identifiers, tenant/workspace scope, per-action failure counts, latency, retries, and any same-window successful bot-token Slack actions for controlled comparison?

What exact connection/auth configuration changed, if anything, for the affected Slack connection before the incident: user_scopes vs bot scopes, reconnect/install time, selected connected account, credential version/refresh events, app/workspace policy signals, and any nearby tool-executor deploy or config change affecting Slack auth handling?

Does the evidence show the failed executions used a user token lacking the required user scope while bot-token actions remained healthy, versus alternatives such as wrong connected account, revoked consent, workspace policy block, refresh/credential regression, or an internal executor change misrouting token selection?
Challenge the diagnosis, evidence grounding and verification gaps.
Write the evidence-backed internal report and proposed next steps.

objections: The evidence proves the immediate failure mechanism for the observed cedar execution—user-token call executed with empty user scopes and returned missing_scope—but does not prove why user_scopes were empty in production.
The complaint's 'bot posting continued to work' portion is not directly verified by a same-window cedar bot-post success record; current evidence only shows another tenant's Slack path was healthy.

events.question: Using null-filter queries first, what canonical executor records exist for the failed Slack user-token actions between 2026-11-12T09:50:00Z and 2026-11-12T10:15:00Z, including exact error payloads (for example missing_scope), request/connection identifiers, tenant/workspace scope, per-action failure counts, latency, retries, and any same-window successful bot-token Slack actions for controlled comparison?

notes: Observed auth config at failure time for cedar used a user-token action (`required_token_kind: "user"`) but had `auth_config_user_scopes: []` while `auth_config_bot_scopes: ["search:read"]`; the canonical failing executor log shows `missing_scope` 403, and the controlled sandbox comparison passes only when `user_scopes` is changed to include `search:read` with bot scopes unchanged. Citations: ev_0e985d9e82d6/slack-user-043:logs:0; ev_315dcd1e5920/slack-user-043:reproduce:0; ev_315dcd1e5920/slack-user-043:reproduce:1.

I do not see canonical evidence here for what changed before the incident in reconnect/install time, selected connected account, credential version, refresh activity, or Slack workspace/app policy state. Empty time-bounded deployment/dependency queries also do not establish absence of those auth-side events. Citations: ev_f85c41b33996 has no records; ev_321a7a77996d has no records.

Impact appears tenant-isolated to cedar rather than a broad Slack/provider outage: cedar had 400/670 failures (~60%), 400 blocked operations, queue depth 120, p95 1600 ms, while maple had 0/560 failures and normal latency; a maple Slack read also succeeded in the same window. Citations: ev_ef8b2f66c4c8/slack-user-043:metrics:0; ev_ef8b2f66c4c8/slack-user-043:metrics:1; ev_0e985d9e82d6/slack-user-043:logs:1.

No nearby tool-executor deploy/config change is evidenced in the incident window; the only deployment record is an unrelated support-dashboard release at 10:05Z. Dependency telemetry shows provider API reachable, which argues against a general provider reachability failure but not against missing auth-side history. Citations: ev_387a4b1218f7/slack-user-043:deployments:0; ev_5101fee03862/slack-user-043:dependencies:0.

Canonical executor log evidence in-window shows one failed Slack user-token action for tenant cedar at 2026-11-12T10:05:00Z: request_id req-43, toolkit slack, status 403, required_token_kind user, auth_config_bot_scopes [search:read], auth_config_user_scopes [], error missing_scope. No connection_id or workspace_id appears in the canonical executor record provided. Citations: ev_81d94d9c517b/slack-user-043:logs:0.

Affected-tenant metrics at the same timestamp show cedar had 670 requests with 400 failures (59.7% failure rate), 400 business operations blocked, queue_depth 120, and p95_latency_ms 1600. The provided canonical records do not break the 400 failures down by Slack action name, and no retry-count field is present, so per-action counts and retries are not directly observed. Citations: ev_63fcf219c68a/slack-user-043:metrics:0.

Controlled comparison in the same window/stack: tenant maple has a successful executor record at 2026-11-12T10:05:00Z with status 200 and flags same_provider_available=true, unrelated_read_succeeds=true; maple metrics show 560 requests, 0 failures, queue_depth 0, p95_latency_ms 160. This supports tenant-isolated impact rather than a broad executor/provider outage, but the success record does not explicitly identify a bot-token Slack posting action. Citations: ev_021b3a6173e6/slack-user-043:logs:1; ev_ef8b2f66c4c8/slack-user-043:metrics:1.

Important gaps: no canonical executor record in the supplied evidence explicitly shows a same-window successful bot-token Slack action, no workspace/connection identifier is present, and no retry telemetry is exposed. Dependency context says provider_api_reachable=true, which is consistent with reachability but not a proof of provider-side success for the failed request. Citation: ev_5101fee03862/slack-user-043:dependencies:0.

events.question: Does the evidence show the failed executions used a user token lacking the required user scope while bot-token actions remained healthy, versus alternatives such as wrong connected account, revoked consent, workspace policy block, refresh/credential regression, or an internal executor change misrouting token selection?

notes: Best-supported conclusion: the observed failed executions used a user-token path lacking the required user scope.
The evidence is weaker for the specific claim that bot-token posting remained healthy, because no canonical same-window bot-post success record is supplied.

Alternatives such as revoked consent, workspace policy block, wrong connected account, or internal token misrouting are not supported directly by the supplied canonical telemetry, though account-selection remains a material gap.

hypothesis.description: The observed cedar failures are most consistent with Slack user-token actions executing without the required user scope configured. The failing executor record shows a user-token action with empty user scopes and a 403 missing_scope, while a controlled comparison succeeds when only user_scopes is corrected to include search:read.
assumptions: This explains the observed failed cedar execution and likely a substantial share of cedar's failures, but the provided metrics do not break all 400 failures down by action.
The evidence supports tenant-isolated Slack auth misconfiguration more strongly than a broad provider or executor outage.
The supplied canonical evidence does not itself prove a same-window successful bot-token posting action for cedar; it only shows another tenant's Slack read path remained healthy.

findings.statement: The canonical failing executor record for cedar required a user token, had bot scopes present but no user scopes, and failed with Slack missing_scope (403).

In a controlled reproduction, the original configuration with empty user_scopes failed with missing_scope, and the otherwise same request passed only after adding search:read to user_scopes; bot scopes were unchanged.

Impact appears isolated to cedar: cedar saw 400 failures out of 670 requests with 400 blocked operations, queue depth 120, and p95 latency 1600 ms, while maple had 0 failures out of 560 requests and normal latency.
A comparison tenant had a successful Slack-related read in the same window, and dependency context shows provider API reachability, which argues against a broad Slack/provider reachability outage.

The supplied canonical records do not include workspace/connection identity, reconnect history, or a same-window successful bot-token posting record, so they do not fully rule out account-selection or explain the reported bot-posting health claim directly.

actions: Configure the required Slack user_scopes for the affected user-token action; bot scopes alone do not authorize user-token calls.
Reconnect the intended Slack user after adding the required user scope so the grant includes that scope.
Collect canonical telemetry tying the failing request to its workspace/connection and verify which cedar actions used user versus bot tokens.
After scope correction and reconnection, replay or retest the blocked cedar operations that failed with missing_scope.
missing_checks: Obtain a canonical same-window record for the reported healthy bot-token posting path to directly verify the 'bot posting continued to work' portion of the complaint.
Obtain canonical connection/workspace/account identifiers for the failed cedar request to fully exclude wrong connected account as the reason user scopes were empty.

hypothesis.description: A secondary possibility is that the failing cedar execution selected a different Slack connected account whose user grant lacked the required scope. This could also produce empty observed user scopes and missing_scope, but no canonical account-selection evidence is provided.
assumptions: This is an alternative explanation for why user_scopes were empty, not a different immediate failure mechanism.
The controlled comparison shows scope presence is sufficient to make the request pass, but does not identify why the live cedar request lacked user scopes.

findings.statement: The live cedar failure shows the selected auth configuration for a user-token action had no user scopes and returned missing_scope.

The controlled comparison confirms that adding the user scope is sufficient to succeed, but it does not reveal whether the empty user scopes in production came from intentional configuration or from choosing the wrong connected account.
No canonical record includes connection_id, workspace_id, or account-selection traces, so account mismatch cannot be fully excluded from the supplied evidence.

actions: Verify which Slack connected account/workspace was selected for req-43 and compare it with the intended cedar account.
If the wrong account was selected, switch the workflow to the intended connected account/project connection.
Add canonical logging of connection/account identifiers for Slack executions so future missing-scope incidents can distinguish misconfiguration from account mismatch.
missing_checks: Canonical account-selection or connection-identity records for the failed cedar request.

hypothesis.description: Workspace policy or consent revocation is less consistent with the observed data. Those paths could block or reduce granted scopes, but the supplied canonical evidence shows a straightforward empty-user-scope configuration at execution time and does not contain policy-block or revoked-consent signals.
assumptions: This candidate groups unobserved policy/consent alternatives because neither has direct canonical support here.
A policy or consent issue could still be an upstream reason the user grant ended up without scope, but that is not demonstrated in the supplied records.

findings.statement: The observed live failure is missing_scope on a user-token action whose execution-time auth config had no user scopes, which more directly fits scope configuration than a session-policy or provider outage mechanism.
The dependency list includes session-policy as a dependency, but there is no canonical record showing a workspace policy block or consent-revoked error for the failed request.

actions: Check Slack workspace/app governance and grant state only if scope correction alone does not explain why the user grant lacked the required scope.
If needed, have a workspace admin verify the app installation and whether the custom OAuth app/user grant is permitted and still approved.
Capture canonical consent/policy diagnostics alongside executor failures to distinguish absent scopes from blocked grants.
missing_checks: Canonical Slack auth/policy records showing whether the cedar user grant was revoked, reduced, or blocked by workspace policy.

findings.statement: The failed cedar execution used a Slack user-token action and failed with missing_scope while auth_config_user_scopes was empty and auth_config_bot_scopes contained search:read.
A controlled original-versus-corrected comparison isolates the variable: empty user_scopes reproduces missing_scope, while adding search:read to user_scopes makes the same request succeed.
Observed production impact was significant but tenant-isolated: cedar had 400/670 failures with backlog and elevated latency, while maple had 0/560 failures and normal latency.
A same-window maple executor record succeeded, supporting isolation to cedar rather than a platform-wide Slack failure.
No tool-executor deployment is evidenced in the incident window; the only deployment record is an unrelated support-dashboard release.
Dependency context shows provider API reachability, which is consistent with the request reaching an auth/provider boundary rather than failing from general provider unreachability.

The supplied canonical evidence does not include connection/workspace/account identity or a same-window successful bot-posting record, so it cannot fully settle wrong-account selection or directly prove the reported healthy bot-posting path.

The missing checks about same-window bot success and connection/workspace identity are useful reassurance and better root-cause attribution, but they would not materially overturn the observed immediate mechanism for req-43.
It is appropriate to keep wrong_connected_account and workspace_app_policy as secondary unverified explanations for why the scope set was empty, not as blockers to the bounded probable diagnosis.

findings.statement: The failed cedar execution required a Slack user token, had bot scopes present but no user scopes configured, and returned 403 missing_scope.

In controlled sandbox telemetry, the original configuration with empty user_scopes failed with missing_scope, while the otherwise same request succeeded after adding search:read to user_scopes; bot scopes were unchanged.

Observed impact was significant and tenant-scoped: cedar had 670 requests with 400 failures, 400 blocked business operations, queue depth 120, and p95 latency 1600 ms, while maple had 560 requests with 0 failures and p95 latency 160 ms.
A same-window maple executor record succeeded, supporting isolation to cedar rather than a platform-wide Slack failure.
Dependency context shows provider API reachability, which is consistent with an auth/scope problem rather than a broad provider reachability outage.
No tool-executor deployment is evidenced in the incident window; the only observed deployment record is an unrelated support-dashboard release.

The supplied canonical evidence does not include connection/workspace/account identity or a same-window successful cedar bot-posting record, so it cannot fully distinguish wrong-account selection or directly verify the reported healthy bot-posting path.
